name: Software as a Medical Device
title: Software as a Medical Device
answer: Software as a Medical Device refers to software intended for medical purposes without being part of a hardware medical device. It includes diagnostic algorithms, dose calculators, monitoring apps, and clinical decision support. The site tracks 1000 medical AI models, many of which fall under SaMD when they perform or guide clinical tasks. Scope covers regulatory classification, quality systems, and postmarket surveillance.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: SaMD runs on general-purpose computing platforms such as servers, cloud services, mobile devices, and hospital workstations, rather than dedicated embedded hardware. It depends on standard software infrastructure: operating systems, data pipelines, model serving frameworks, and electronic health record integrations. Security controls include encryption, access management, audit logging, and vulnerability patching. Because the device is software, updates can be distributed remotely, but each change must be assessed for impact on safety and performance.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Development follows a risk-based lifecycle under standards such as IEC 62304 for software life cycle processes and ISO 14971 for risk management. Teams define intended use, identify hazards, and build traceability from requirements through design, code, and verification. Clinical evaluation may use retrospective data, prospective studies, or algorithm validation against reference standards. For AI-based SaMD, model training, data curation, and performance monitoring are part of the controlled design process.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: SaMD is regulated by bodies such as the US FDA, which classifies devices by risk and requires premarket submissions or clearance for many products. Manufacturers must maintain a quality management system, report adverse events, and manage recalls. The site tracks 210 compliance and regulation pages and 6 active product liability and wrongful death lawsuits against AI companies, reflecting the legal exposure when software fails or harms patients. Data privacy rules, such as HIPAA in the US, also apply to patient data processed by SaMD.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward continuous learning systems, where models update after deployment, and toward greater use of foundation models in clinical workflows. Regulators are developing frameworks for predetermined change control plans and real-world performance monitoring. The site's tracking of 1000 medical AI models and 732 AI tools suggests rapid growth, but harmonized global standards and clearer liability rules remain open. Expect more emphasis on interoperability, explainability, and postmarket evidence as SaMD becomes embedded in routine care.
